claim: Phosphorylation of Aurora A on T288 leads to a ~100 fold increase in catalytic activity.
source: We set out to explain how phosphorylation of AurA on T288 leads to a ~100 fold increase in catalytic activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) (Zorba et al., 2014; Dodson and Bayliss, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Zorba et al., 2014; Dodson and Bayliss, 2012) and reference to experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Tpx2 binding triggers a conformational change from the DFG-Out to the DFG-In state in Aurora A.
source: We previously used an infrared (IR) probe that tracks the DFG motif of AurA to show that Tpx2 binding triggers a conformational change from the DFG-Out to the DFG-In state (Cyphers et al., 2017), resulting in the assembly of the active site and the regulatory spine (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Cyphers et al., 2017) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: IR spectra of nitrile-labeled phosphorylated Aurora A showed predominantly a single absorbance band centered at 2158 cm−1.
source: IR spectra of nitrile-labeled phosphorylated AurA showed predominantly a single absorbance band centered at 2158 cm−1 (Figure 1a, solid black line).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental IR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The peak at 2158 cm−1 in IR spectra of Aurora A corresponds to the DFG-Out form of the kinase.
source: We previously assigned this peak in IR spectra of unphosphorylated AurA to the DFG-Out form of the kinase, in which the nitrile probe is buried in a hydrophobic pocket (Figure 1b, lower panel) (Cyphers et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Cyphers et al., 2017) and reference to structural data in Figure 1b.

claim: Addition of saturating amounts of Tpx2 peptide to phosphorylated Aurora A causes the central IR peak at 2158 cm−1 to be largely replaced by two new peaks at 2149 cm−1 and 2164 cm−1.
source: Addition of saturating amounts of Tpx2 peptide (residues 1–43 of human Tpx2) to the IR samples caused a dramatic spectral change wherein the central peak at 2158 cm−1 is largely replaced by two new peaks at 2149 cm−1 and 2164 cm−1 (Figure 1a, dashed black line).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental IR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The IR spectral changes upon Tpx2 binding are indicative of a shift to the DFG-In state.
source: These changes are indicative of a shift to the DFG-In state, in which water molecules coordinated to the DFG motif form hydrogen bonds to the nitrile probe, causing pronounced spectral shifts (Figure 1b, upper right panel) (Cyphers et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Cyphers et al., 2017) and reference to structural data in Figure 1b.

claim: The W277A mutation causes a clear spectral shift of the 2158 cm−1 peak in IR spectra of Aurora A.
source: IR spectra of the W277A mutant showed a clear spectral shift of the 2158 cm−1 peak (Figure 1c), consistent with this peak arising from the DFG-Out state.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental IR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Phosphorylation of Aurora A on T288 does not substantially change the DFG-In/Out equilibrium.
source: These IR results suggested that phosphorylation alone does not substantially change the DFG-In/Out equilibrium of AurA, unlike Tpx2 binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the IR spectroscopy results described in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: Phosphorylated Aurora A exhibits robust catalytic activity in the absence of Tpx2 and is further activated ~4 fold by the addition of Tpx2.
source: the labeled phosphorylated sample exhibited robust catalytic activity in the absence of Tpx2, and was further activated ~4 fold by the addition of Tpx2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c) (Zorba et al., 2014; Dodson and Bayliss, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental kinase activity data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c and citations to prior work (Zorba et al., 2014; Dodson and Bayliss, 2012).

claim: The distance distributions measured by FRET for phosphorylated and unphosphorylated Aurora A in the absence of ligands are strikingly similar.
source: The distance distributions measured for the phosphorylated and unphosphorylated kinase in the absence of ligands are strikingly similar (Figure 2b, bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-resolved FRET data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: A broad distance distribution centered around ~30 angstroms is observed for apo Aurora A regardless of phosphorylation state, indicating that the activation loop is highly flexible.
source: In both cases, a broad distribution centered around ~30 angstroms is observed for apo AurA, indicating that the activation loop is highly flexible regardless of the phosphorylation state (Figure 2b, black).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-resolved FRET data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: When phosphorylated and unphosphorylated Aurora A samples are saturated with both Tpx2 peptide and nucleotide, narrow distance distributions shifted to ~54 angstroms are observed.
source: In contrast, when the phosphorylated and unphosphorylated samples were saturated with both Tpx2 peptide and nucleotide (either ADP or the non-hydrolysable ATP-analog AMPPNP), narrow distributions were observed that were shifted to ~54 angstroms (Figure 2b, blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-resolved FRET data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The narrow distance distributions at ~54 angstroms indicate adoption of a well-defined structure consistent with the DFG-In state.
source: This indicates adoption of a well-defined structure consistent with the DFG-In state, in which the segment of the loop containing the labeling site is anchored to the C-terminal lobe of the kinase by flanking β-sheet interactions (Bayliss et al., 2003) (Figure 2a, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-resolved FRET data and citation to structural data (Bayliss et al., 2003) shown in Figure 2a.

claim: ADP binds to phosphorylated and unphosphorylated Aurora A with similar affinities.
source: Importantly, ADP bound to phosphorylated and unphosphorylated AurA with similar affinities (Figure 2c, top left panel), indicating that the interaction of the kinase with nucleotide is not substantially affected by phosphorylation on the activation loop.
evidence: The claim is supported by equilibrium dissociation constant measurements shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Tpx2 enhances the binding affinity of nucleotides to both unphosphorylated and phosphorylated Aurora A.
source: In contrast, Tpx2, which does trigger a conformational change from the DFG-Out to the DFG-In state in both unphosphorylated and phosphorylated AurA, also enhances the binding affinity of nucleotides in both cases (Figure 2c, compare top panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by equilibrium dissociation constant measurements shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Phosphorylation substantially enhances the binding of Tpx2 to Aurora A, increasing the affinity by a factor of ~20.
source: While phosphorylation does not affect nucleotide binding to apo AurA, we found that it does substantially enhance the binding of Tpx2 to the exterior surface of the kinase, increasing the affinity by a factor of ~20 (Figure 2c, bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by equilibrium dissociation constant measurements shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Once Tpx2 is bound, phosphorylation leads to an enhancement of nucleotide affinity.
source: In addition, once Tpx2 is bound, phosphorylation does lead to an enhancement of nucleotide affinity (Figure 2c, top right panel, compare red and blue), indicating that allosteric coupling between the phosphorylation site and the active site, missing in apo AurA, is established in the AurA:Tpx2 complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by equilibrium dissociation constant measurements shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations of wild-type Aurora A remained predominantly in the initial DFG-In state.
source: Analysis of the DFG conformation revealed that the simulations remained predominantly in their initial DFG-In state (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the simulation time was insufficient to capture the slow conformational change to the DFG-Out state.
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phosphorylated Aurora A is locked into a single conformation with a long L225-S284 distance (42 Å) and short R255-T288 distance (~5 Å) in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: In striking contrast, the simulations showed that phosphorylated AurA is locked into a single conformation with a long L225-S284 distance (42 Å, cf. 41 Å in the 1OL5 x-ray structure) and short R255-T288 distance (~5 Å, cf. 5.5 Å in 1OL5), indicative of a stable active state in which the loop is fully ordered and the phosphothreonine residue forms ion-pairing interactions with R255 and R180 (Figure 3b, bottom left panel, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Unphosphorylated Aurora A without Tpx2 shows two discrete subpopulations in molecular dynamics simulations: one corresponding to the active-like state with a long L225-S284 distance (~43 Å), and another with a much shorter distance (~38 Å).
source: Although unphosphorylated AurA is highly dynamic in the absence of Tpx2, the activation loop is not in fact disordered in the simulations. Instead, two discrete subpopulations are observed: one subpopulation corresponding to the active-like state with a long L225-S284 distance (~43 Å), and another with a much shorter distance (~38 Å), representing a DFG-In conformation in which the activation loop is not correctly positioned for catalytic function (Figure 3b, lower right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In the autoinhibited DFG-In subpopulation, the tip of the activation loop folds into a short helical turn spanning residues P282-R286.
source: Manual inspection of the trajectories revealed that in this subpopulation the tip of the activation loop folds into a short helical turn spanning residues P282-R286, with the P282 proline residue serving as the N-terminal capping residue (Kumar and Bansal, 1998) in most of the trajectories (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 3c and citation to prior work (Kumar and Bansal, 1998).

claim: The R180A mutant of Aurora A possesses 4-fold lower activity in the absence of Tpx2, whereas the activity in the presence of Tpx2 is only modestly affected.
source: The R180A mutant possessed 4-fold lower activity in the absence of Tpx2, whereas the activity in the presence of Tpx2 was only modestly affected (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: DEER spectra acquired for phosphorylated Aurora A bound to ADP or AMPPNP showed a rapidly decaying and heavily damped signal, consistent with the activation loop adopting multiple conformations.
source: DEER spectra acquired for the phosphorylated kinase bound to ADP or AMPPNP showed a rapidly decaying and heavily damped signal, consistent with the activation loop adopting multiple conformations (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a, blue lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by DEER spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: DEER spectra of phosphorylated Aurora A bound to Tpx2 decayed much less rapidly and exhibited pronounced oscillations, indicating increased spin-spin distance and a high degree of structural order.
source: However, DEER spectra of phosphorylated AurA bound to Tpx2 decayed much less rapidly, indicating increased spin-spin distance, and exhibited pronounced oscillations, indicating a high degree of structural order (Figure 4a, yellow).
evidence: The claim is supported by DEER spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The distance distribution for phosphorylated Aurora A bound to Tpx2 displayed a single dominant peak at 52 angstroms.
source: The corresponding distance distribution displayed a single dominant peak at 52 angstroms (Figure 4b, yellow), representing a ~5 angstrom longer mean spin-spin distance than seen in the samples lacking Tpx2, consistent with the activation loop now adopting the extended DFG-In conformation (see Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by DEER spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: DEER experiments show that distances beyond 50 angstroms are more populated in phosphorylated Aurora A bound to ADP compared to unphosphorylated Aurora A bound to ADP.
source: However, close inspection of the DEER spectra revealed subtle differences between the unphosphorylated and phosphorylated samples (Figure 4a inset), and the corresponding distributions indicated that distances beyond 50 angstroms were more populated in the phosphorylated sample (Figure 4b, dark blue shading).
evidence: The claim is supported by DEER spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4b.

claim: DEER spectra measured on unphosphorylated and phosphorylated Aurora A bound to SNS-314 showed pronounced oscillations with differing periods, indicating that both samples adopt well-defined structures with different major spin-spin distances.
source: Strikingly, DEER spectra measured on unphosphorylated and phosphorylated AurA bound to SNS-314 showed pronounced oscillations with differing periods, indicating that both samples adopt well-defined structures, but that the major spin-spin distances are different in the two cases (Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is supported by DEER spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The Tikhonov distributions for Aurora A bound to SNS-314 showed sharp peaks at 49 and 53 angstroms for the unphosphorylated and phosphorylated kinase, respectively.
source: Indeed, the Tikhonov distributions showed sharp peaks at 49 and 53 angstroms for the unphosphorylated and phosphorylated kinase, respectively (Figure 4e, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by DEER spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Phosphorylation triggers a switch from an autoinhibited DFG-In substate to an active DFG-In substate in Aurora A.
source: We conclude that while phosphorylated AurA samples the DFG-Out and DFG-In states to a similar extent as the unphosphorylated kinase, the structure and dynamics of the DFG-In subpopulation are profoundly altered by phosphorylation, leading to catalytic activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of IR, FRET, DEER, and molecular dynamics simulations described throughout the Results section.

claim: Aurora A is an essential mitotic protein that controls a variety of cellular processes including mitotic spindle assembly, centrosome maturation, and mitotic entry.
source: The serine/threonine kinase Aurora A (AurA) is an essential mitotic protein that controls a variety of cellular processes including mitotic spindle assembly, centrosome maturation, and mitotic entry (Glover et al., 1995; Hannak et al., 2001; Berdnik and Knoblich, 2002; Macůrek et al., 2008; Seki et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Glover et al., 1995; Hannak et al., 2001; Berdnik and Knoblich, 2002; Macůrek et al., 2008; Seki et al., 2008).

claim: At the centrosome, Aurora A must first be activated by autophosphorylation on the activation loop threonine residue T288 in order to carry out its centrosomal functions.
source: At the centrosome, AurA must first be activated by autophosphorylation on the activation loop threonine residue T288 in order to carry out its centrosomal functions.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Aurora A function.

claim: At the mitotic spindle, Aurora A is activated by binding to the spindle assembly factor Tpx2.
source: At the mitotic spindle, AurA is instead activated by binding to the spindle assembly factor Tpx2 (Kufer et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Kufer et al., 2002).

claim: The spindle-associated pool of Aurora A must be maintained in the unphosphorylated state by the phosphatase PP6 in order for spindle assembly to proceed faithfully.
source: This spindle-associated pool of AurA must be maintained in the unphosphorylated state by the phosphatase PP6 in order for spindle assembly to proceed faithfully (Zeng et al., 2010; Toya et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Zeng et al., 2010; Toya et al., 2011).

claim: Tpx2 and phosphorylation can act independently to increase Aurora A kinase activity by up to several hundred-fold.
source: Extensive in vitro studies have confirmed that Tpx2 and phosphorylation can act independently to increase AurA kinase activity by up to several hundred-fold (Zorba et al., 2014; Dodson and Bayliss, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Zorba et al., 2014; Dodson and Bayliss, 2012).

claim: Crystal structures of phosphorylated Aurora A bound to Tpx2 show the T288 phosphothreonine residue forming canonical ionic interactions.
source: Since crystal structures of phosphorylated AurA bound to Tpx2 show the T288 phosphothreonine residue forming the canonical ionic interactions thought to stabilize the DFG-In state (Bayliss et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2009), it has been assumed that phosphorylation also triggers a transition from the DFG-Out to the DFG-In state.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior structural work (Bayliss et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2009).

claim: Phosphorylation on a specific site in the activation loop of the kinase domain is the most widely conserved regulatory mechanism in kinases.
source: Phosphorylation on a specific site in the activation loop of the kinase domain is the most widely conserved regulatory mechanism in kinases (Johnson et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Johnson et al., 1996).

claim: X-ray structures show that ionic interactions between the phosphate moiety and a surrounding pocket of basic residues stabilize the activation loop in a conserved active conformation.
source: X-ray structures show that ionic interactions between the phosphate moiety and a surrounding pocket of basic residues stabilize the activation loop in a conserved active conformation (Knighton et al., 1991; Yamaguchi and Hendrickson, 1996; Steichen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior structural work (Knighton et al., 1991; Yamaguchi and Hendrickson, 1996; Steichen et al., 2012).

claim: In the active state, a catalytic asp-phe-gly (DFG) motif at the N-terminal end of the activation loop adopts an active 'DFG-In' conformation.
source: In this active state, a catalytic asp-phe-gly (DFG) motif at the N-terminal end of the activation loop adopts an active 'DFG-In' conformation, with the aspartate residue of the DFG motif pointing into the active site to coordinate Mg-ATP, and the C-terminal segment of the activation loop positioned to bind peptide substrates.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about kinase structure and function.

claim: The DFG-In state is stabilized by the assembly of a network of hydrophobic residues, termed the regulatory spine.
source: The DFG-In state is stabilized by the assembly of a network of hydrophobic residues, termed the regulatory spine, that lock together the N-terminal lobe, the αC-helix, the DFG motif and the C-terminal lobe of the kinase (Kornev et al., 2006; Kornev et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kornev et al., 2006; Kornev et al., 2008).

claim: An important autoinhibited state, called 'DFG-Out', involves a flip in the backbone torsion angles of the DFG motif.
source: An important autoinhibited state, called 'DFG-Out', involves a flip in the backbone torsion angles of the DFG motif, reorienting the DFG aspartate out of the active site to prevent magnesium coordination, repositioning the activation loop to block peptide binding, and disassembling the regulatory spine (Hubbard et al., 1994; Nagar et al., 2003; Mol et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hubbard et al., 1994; Nagar et al., 2003; Mol et al., 2004).

claim: Selective recognition of the DFG-Out state underlies the mechanism of action of many small-molecule kinase inhibitors.
source: This conformational change dramatically alters the chemical makeup of the active site, and selective recognition of the DFG-Out state underlies the mechanism of action of many small-molecule kinase inhibitors (Liu and Gray, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Liu and Gray, 2006).

claim: Disruption of kinase regulatory mechanisms, leading to constitutive kinase activity, is a major cause of human cancer.
source: Disruption of these mechanisms, leading to constitutive kinase activity, is a major cause of human cancer, and small molecules that inhibit specific disease-associated kinases are an increasingly important component of many modern cancer therapies (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Zhang et al., 2009).

claim: The majority of eukaryotic protein kinases are activated by phosphorylation on the activation loop at a site equivalent to T288 in Aurora A.
source: The majority of eukaryotic protein kinases are activated by phosphorylation on the activation loop at a site equivalent to T288 in AurA (Johnson et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Johnson et al., 1996).

claim: Phosphorylation and Tpx2 activate Aurora A through quite different albeit complementary mechanisms.
source: Thus it appears that phosphorylation and Tpx2 activate AurA through quite different - albeit complementary - mechanisms, with phosphorylation triggering a structural switch within the DFG-In subpopulation, and Tpx2 instead promoting a DFG flip to increase the population of the DFG-In state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of the study.

claim: Phosphorylation triggers a structural switch within the DFG-In subpopulation of Aurora A.
source: Thus it appears that phosphorylation and Tpx2 activate AurA through quite different - albeit complementary - mechanisms, with phosphorylation triggering a structural switch within the DFG-In subpopulation, and Tpx2 instead promoting a DFG flip to increase the population of the DFG-In state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of the study.

claim: Tpx2 promotes a DFG flip to increase the population of the DFG-In state in Aurora A.
source: Thus it appears that phosphorylation and Tpx2 activate AurA through quite different - albeit complementary - mechanisms, with phosphorylation triggering a structural switch within the DFG-In subpopulation, and Tpx2 instead promoting a DFG flip to increase the population of the DFG-In state.
evidence: The claim is supported by prior work (Cyphers et al., 2017) and the current study's results.

claim: The AGC kinases possess a C-terminal hydrophobic motif that docks in cis onto a pocket above the αC-helix in a manner that closely resembles the interaction of Tpx2 with Aurora A.
source: The AGC kinases possess a C-terminal hydrophobic motif that docks in cis onto a pocket above the αC-helix in a manner that closely resembles the interaction of Tpx2 with AurA (Frödin et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2002b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Frödin et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2002b).

claim: Activation of the AGC kinases by activation loop phosphorylation and hydrophobic motif engagement are tightly coupled events.
source: Activation of the AGC kinases by activation loop phosphorylation and hydrophobic motif engagement are tightly coupled events (Alessi et al., 1996) and are both important for activation (Batkin et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Alessi et al., 1996; Batkin et al., 2000).

claim: The contrasting ability of Aurora A to be independently activated by phosphorylation or Tpx2 is dependent upon a unique active-site water network that strengthens the regulatory spine of the kinase relative to that of the AGC kinases.
source: The contrasting ability of AurA to be independently activated by phosphorylation or Tpx2 is dependent upon a unique active-site water network that strengthens the regulatory spine of the kinase relative to that of the AGC kinases (Cyphers et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Cyphers et al., 2017).

claim: Mutational inactivation of the PP6 phosphatase in ~10% of melanoma patients leads to accumulation of phosphorylated Aurora A bound to Tpx2 on the mitotic spindle.
source: The doubly-activated form of the kinase is prominent, however, in the tumors of ~10% of melanoma patients, where mutational inactivation of the PP6 phosphatase leads to accumulation of phosphorylated AurA bound to Tpx2 on the mitotic spindle, resulting in chromosome instability and DNA damage that can be partially reversed by AurA inhibitors (Hammond et al., 2013; Hodis et al., 2012; Gold et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hammond et al., 2013; Hodis et al., 2012; Gold et al., 2014).

claim: Many other protein kinases, including non-receptor and receptor tyrosine kinases and the cyclin-dependent kinases, employ an autoinhibitory DFG-In state for regulatory control.
source: It is noteworthy that many other protein kinases, including non-receptor and receptor tyrosine kinases (Wood et al., 2004; Xu et al., 1997) and the cyclin-dependent kinases (De Bondt et al., 1993), employ an autoinhibitory DFG-In state, as opposed to the DFG-Out state, for regulatory control.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Wood et al., 2004; Xu et al., 1997; De Bondt et al., 1993).

claim: The ~100 fold activation of Aurora A by phosphorylation occurs without a population shift from the DFG-Out to the DFG-In state.
source: Here we use a battery of spectroscopic methods that track different catalytic elements of the kinase domain to show that the ~100 fold activation of the mitotic kinase Aurora A (AurA) by phosphorylation occurs without a population shift from the DFG-Out to the DFG-In state, and that the activation loop of the activated kinase remains highly dynamic.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined results of IR, FRET, and DEER experiments described in the Results section.

claim: The activation loop of phosphorylated Aurora A remains highly dynamic.
source: Here we use a battery of spectroscopic methods that track different catalytic elements of the kinase domain to show that the ~100 fold activation of the mitotic kinase Aurora A (AurA) by phosphorylation occurs without a population shift from the DFG-Out to the DFG-In state, and that the activation loop of the activated kinase remains highly dynamic.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined results of IR, FRET, and DEER experiments described in the Results section.

claim: Phosphorylation triggers a switch within the DFG-In subpopulation from an autoinhibited DFG-In substate to an active DFG-In substate, leading to catalytic activation.
source: Instead, molecular dynamics simulations and electron paramagnetic resonance experiments show that phosphorylation triggers a switch within the DFG-In subpopulation from an autoinhibited DFG-In substate to an active DFG-In substate, leading to catalytic activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulations and EPR (DEER) experiments described in the Results section.

claim: A recent single-molecule fluorescence study reported that phosphorylated Aurora A dynamically transitions between multiple structural states.
source: Of note, a recent single-molecule fluorescence study also reported that phosphorylated AurA dynamically transitions between multiple structural states (Gilburt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Gilburt et al., 2017).

claim: Phosphorylated Aurora A interacts with Cep-192, Bora, and Ajuba at the centrosome, and these interactions can further regulate Aurora A activity towards specific substrates.
source: For instance, phosphorylated AurA has been shown to interact with Cep-192 (Joukov et al., 2014), Bora (Macůrek et al., 2008; Seki et al., 2008), and Ajuba (Hirota et al., 2003) at the centrosome, and these interactions can further regulate AurA activity towards specific substrates.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Joukov et al., 2014; Macůrek et al., 2008; Seki et al., 2008; Hirota et al., 2003).

claim: The oncogenic transcription factor N-Myc binds to Aurora A through a pseudosubstrate interaction and stabilizes the phosphorylated kinase in the active conformation.
source: In this context it is noteworthy that the oncogenic transcription factor N-Myc binds to AurA through a pseudosubstrate interaction, and does indeed appear to stabilize the phosphorylated kinase in the active conformation (Richards et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Richards et al., 2016).

claim: The Tpx2-bound spindle pool of Aurora A is thought to be predominantly unphosphorylated in normal cells.
source: It is unclear whether activation of AurA by both phosphorylation and Tpx2 occurs in normal cells, where the Tpx2-bound spindle pool of AurA is thought to be predominantly unphosphorylated (Zeng et al., 2010; Toya et al., 2011), and the centrosomal pool is not bound to Tpx2 (Kufer et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Zeng et al., 2010; Toya et al., 2011).

claim: The centrosomal pool of Aurora A is not bound to Tpx2.
source: It is unclear whether activation of AurA by both phosphorylation and Tpx2 occurs in normal cells, where the Tpx2-bound spindle pool of AurA is thought to be predominantly unphosphorylated (Zeng et al., 2010; Toya et al., 2011), and the centrosomal pool is not bound to Tpx2 (Kufer et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Kufer et al., 2002).

claim: The formation of short helices in the activation loop is a common feature of the inactive states of other protein kinases.
source: Although this conformation has not been observed in X-ray structures of AurA, the formation of short helices in the activation loop is a common feature of the inactive states of other protein kinases (Sicheri et al., 1997; Wood et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2010; De Bondt et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Sicheri et al., 1997; Wood et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2010; De Bondt et al., 1993).

claim: SNS-314 preferentially binds to the DFG-In state of Aurora A.
source: To test this, we used the ATP-competitive AurA inhibitor SNS-314, which preferentially binds to the DFG-In state of AurA (Oslob et al., 2008) (Figure 4d), to induce a homogeneous population of DFG-In kinase.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Oslob et al., 2008) and reference to Figure 4d.

claim: The 4-angstrom increase in spin-spin distance observed in DEER experiments with L225/S284 labeling sites is similar to the difference in L225-S284 Cα distances predicted by MD simulations for the autoinhibited and active DFG-In substates.
source: Interestingly, the 4-angstrom increase in spin-spin distance observed in the DEER experiments performed with the L225/S284 labeling sites (Figure 4e inset) is similar to the difference in the L225-S284 Cα distances predicted by the MD simulations for the autoinhibited and active DFG-In substates (Figure 3b, bottom right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of DEER data (Figure 4e) and MD simulation data (Figure 3b).

claim: The stabilizing ionic interactions between the phosphothreonine and the arginine residues are offset by an energetic penalty associated with refolding the activation loop into the active configuration.
source: The fact that this does not substantially change the DFG equilibrium suggests that the stabilizing ionic interactions between the phosphothreonine and the arginine residues (see Figure 3a) are offset by an energetic penalty associated with refolding the activation loop into the active configuration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that phosphorylation does not shift the DFG equilibrium despite forming stabilizing interactions.

claim: By unfolding the activation loop from the autoinhibited DFG-In state, phosphorylation promotes the formation of the Tpx2-interaction surface by the N-terminal segment of the activation loop, resulting in dramatically enhanced binding affinity.
source: By unfolding the activation loop from the autoinhibited DFG-In state, phosphorylation promotes the formation of the Tpx2-interaction surface by the N-terminal segment of the activation loop, resulting in dramatically enhanced binding affinity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing synergy between phosphorylation and Tpx2.

claim: By binding tightly to the Tpx2-interaction surface, Tpx2 compensates for the energetic cost of reconfiguring the activation loop, allowing the effects of phosphorylation to be manifested as a further stabilization of the active DFG-In state.
source: By binding tightly to this surface, Tpx2 in turn compensates for the energetic cost of reconfiguring the activation loop, allowing the effects of phosphorylation to be manifested as a further stabilization of the active DFG-In state, as we observed in our fluorescence experiments in terms of an additional conformational shift and enhanced nucleotide binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing synergy between phosphorylation and Tpx2.

claim: Phosphorylation can drive catalytic activation of a protein kinase without restraining the protein in the DFG-In state.
source: Our results show that phosphorylation can drive catalytic activation of a protein kinase without restraining the protein in the DFG-In state, providing a contrasting and highly dynamic view of an activated kinase in which major conformational changes of catalytic elements may occur continuously during the catalytic cycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined results of the study.

claim: Phosphorylation is presumably coupled to the αC-helix through the R180 residue.
source: Given that the R180 residue on the αC-helix directly recognizes the pT288 phosphothreonine residue, and that the R180A mutation interferes with activity of the phosphorylated enzyme, phosphorylation is presumably also coupled to the αC-helix.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the R180A mutation data and structural knowledge.

claim: Phosphorylation can be thought of as tuning the free energy surface for the DFG-In state—favoring the active substate over the autoinhibited substate—as opposed to changing the relative free energies of the DFG-In and DFG-Out states.
source: Thus, phosphorylation can be thought of as tuning the free energy surface for the DFG-In state - favoring the active substate over the autoinhibited substate - as opposed to changing the relative free energies of the DFG-In and DFG-Out states.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of the study.

claim: The highly dynamic nature of Aurora A activated only by phosphorylation may be a unique property of the Aurora kinases that reflects the loss of the hydrophobic motif in this lineage.
